intro: Read the deck for the legal text and these notes for what to do with it. Each note explains how to read a slide, what to remember and where organisations slip. Work the examples, answer the recall questions, then start your own data map. This is orientation and not legal advice.

sections.title: Orientation
sections.big_idea: Almost every NGO is a **Data Fiduciary**, and the main duties switch on from 13 May 2027, so the time to take stock is now.
in_plain_words: This part sets the scene. India has a full data-privacy law, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with Rules notified in 2025. It does not exempt non-profits, so any NGO that processes the digital personal data of people in India is covered, with the duties applying from 13 May 2027.

The law switches on in three stages: the Board from 13 November 2025, consent managers from 13 November 2026, and the duties, rights and penalties from 13 May 2027. It rests on seven principles. **Use the self-check to count your gaps**, and remember that this course orients you and does not replace legal advice.

diagram.caption: six streams of personal data in a typical field NGO

key_terms.meaning: The individual the data is about.
Whoever decides why and how the data is processed.
A vendor processing data on your behalf under contract.
Almost anything done with data, from collecting to deleting.
The national regulator that investigates and penalises.

worked_example.title: Score a self-check
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an NGO answers the seven self-check statements on slide 9, saying yes to inventory, consent and access control, and no to the other four.
steps: Count the yes answers: inventory, consent and access control make 3.
Count the gaps (the no answers): 7 − 3 = 4.
The deck says three or more 'no' answers put you where most Indian NGOs are today.
Four is above that line, so the 90-day plan in Part 10 is the right starting point.
worked_example.answer: Four gaps: retention, vendors, grievance and breach plan are the first items to close.

mistakes: Assuming a non-profit is exempt. The Act has no non-profit carve-out.
Treating the course as legal advice for a specific situation, which it states it is not.
Waiting until 2027 to start, when the content of the duties is already fixed.
Forgetting that paper records count once they are typed into Excel or an app.

recall.q: On what date do the main duties, rights and penalties become enforceable?
What are the three stages of commencement?
recall.a: The Board from 13 November 2025, consent managers from 13 November 2026, and the duties, rights and penalties from 13 May 2027.

recall.q: Name the seven principles of the Act.
recall.a: Lawful and transparent use, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, reasonable security and accountability.

recall.q: What role does almost every NGO have under the Act?
recall.a: Data Fiduciary.

sections.title: Why data protection matters
sections.big_idea: A leak harms real people, so data protection is **duty of care** first and compliance second.
in_plain_words: The hypothetical cases in this part show how harm happens: an open spreadsheet link exposes a 4,000-household list, a shared computer exposes survivors' addresses, and a printed HIV client log is photographed for a donor report. In each case a small habit caused a serious harm.

Behind this sits trust and the law. People share the truth only if they believe you will protect it, and the 2017 Puttaswamy judgment made privacy a fundamental right. The Act turns that expectation into a duty. **The higher a field sits on the harm scale, the stronger your reason to collect it at all.**

children.label: Survivor case file
items: Lesson: fewer people, harder to open

children.label: HIV programme client log
items: Lesson: care data stays with care

diagram.caption: three hypothetical cases from the deck

key_terms.meaning: The obligation to avoid making people worse off.
Nine-judge ruling that privacy is a fundamental right.
Using data only for the purpose the person was told.
Beneficiaries often cannot refuse data if aid depends on it.
Up to ₹250 crore for the most serious failures.

worked_example.title: Diagnose the leaked list
worked_example.setup: A livelihoods NGO has a 4,000-household list in a Google Sheet set to 'anyone with the link can view' and pastes the link into a public WhatsApp group.
steps: Ask what was exposed: names, villages, phone numbers, bank numbers and each family's cash-transfer amount.
Ask what the harm was: a moneylender targeted indebted families and two households received fraudulent OTP calls.
Name the duty that failed: reasonable security safeguards, the most heavily penalised duty.
Name the cheap fix: restrict access to named staff and never share a link in a public group.
worked_example.answer: A security failure caused by an open link. The ceiling is ₹250 crore, though the Board sets the actual amount by gravity.

mistakes: Believing a village NGO would be fined ₹250 crore for any slip. That is a ceiling for the worst failures.
Reusing data collected for care in a donor deck or report without fresh, specific consent.
Treating privacy as a cost, when trust drives honest answers and data quality.
Ignoring location and photo data. A recognisable face or house is personal data.

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in Puttaswamy on 24 August 2017?
recall.a: That privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21, with informational privacy included.

recall.q: Why does data quality depend on trust?
recall.a: Where people fear misuse they give false answers, so the evidence base rots.

recall.q: What is the rule of thumb on sensitive data?
recall.a: The higher a row sits on the harm scale, the stronger your justification for collecting it.

recall.q: How fast can you report a breach to the Board?
recall.a: The Rules require a detailed report within 72 hours.

sections.title: Data-protection basics
sections.big_idea: If data can be **linked to a living person**, it is personal data, and it follows a lifecycle you must control at every stage.
in_plain_words: Personal data is any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to it. A name is not needed. A beneficiary ID tied to a name list, a recognisable photo or 'the only widow in ward 3 with a disabled child' all count. Pseudonymised data stays personal because it can be re-linked. Only true anonymisation leaves the law.

The Act covers digital personal data, including paper that is later digitised. It has no separate sensitive category, so one high standard applies. Follow data through collect, store, use, share, retain and delete, and **decide the deletion rule at the design stage**. The seven principles are the memory aid.

diagram.caption: the data lifecycle, stage by stage

key_terms.meaning: Data about an identifiable individual.
Identifiers replaced by a code that can be re-linked; still personal.
No individual can be singled out; outside the Act.
Paper data later entered into a computer; in scope.
Collecting only what the purpose requires.

worked_example.title: Classify five records
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: sort each record into identifiable, pseudonymised or anonymised using the deck's three definitions.
steps: A row with name, phone and village: identifiable, so full duties apply.
'HH-0421' with a lookup table held elsewhere: pseudonymised, still personal because it is reversible.
'62% of 400 households earn below the poverty line': anonymised, since 400 × 0.62 = 248 households are counted as a group.
'The only Dalit woman sarpanch in the block': identifiable even with the name removed, the re-identification trap.
worked_example.answer: Only the aggregate statement is anonymised. The other three are personal data.

mistakes: Thinking that removing the name makes data anonymous.
Relying on the paper loophole for a handwritten book that later gets typed into Excel.
Waiting for the law to label data 'sensitive' instead of judging each field by harm.
Using 'we are small' or 'it is just a spreadsheet' as a reason the Act does not apply.

recall.q: What is the test for personal data?
recall.a: Identifiability: can it be linked back to a specific living person.

recall.q: Why is pseudonymised data still personal?
recall.a: A separate key can re-link the code to the person, so it is reversible.

recall.q: Does the Act define a separate category of sensitive personal data?
recall.a: No. One high standard applies to all personal data, though the Board weighs sensitivity in practice.

recall.q: What is the child age threshold in India compared with the GDPR?
recall.a: Under 18 in India, against 16 in the GDPR with member states allowed to lower it to 13.

sections.title: Meet the DPDP Act 2023
sections.big_idea: The Act is **short, principles-based and phased**, with the detail in the Rules and the duties starting on 13 May 2027.
in_plain_words: The law took over a decade. The 2011 SPDI Rules were weak, the 2017 Puttaswamy ruling required a dedicated law, and the 2019 Bill was withdrawn in 2022. The 2023 Act is shorter and simpler. It covers digital personal data, applies to every kind of organisation, and reaches processing outside India when goods or services are offered to people in India.

The Rules of 13 November 2025 phase commencement in. Some exemptions exist, but they are conditional, and the research exemption fails if data is used for decisions about a specific person. **Read the exemptions as narrow** and confirm dates before any legally significant decision.

events.what: Rules notified; Board and definitions start
Core duties, rights and penalties enforceable

diagram.caption: the enforcement timeline at a glance

key_terms.meaning: 2011 rules under the IT Act for sensitive personal data.
Coverage of processing abroad that serves people in India.
The table of maximum penalties for each failure.
Different Rules start on different dates.
Exemptions, including research, archiving and statistics.

worked_example.title: How long is the runway?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's dates to measure the preparation time from the Rules to the main duties.
steps: The Rules were notified on 13 November 2025 and the main duties start on 13 May 2027.
From 13 November 2025 to 13 November 2026 is 12 months.
From 13 November 2026 to 13 May 2027 is a further 6 months.
Total runway: 12 + 6 = 18 months.
worked_example.answer: 18 months from the Rules to the main duties, and 6 months from the start of consent managers.

mistakes: Assuming the research exemption covers a beneficiary survey that informs who gets a benefit.
Thinking a foreign cloud provider moves your data outside the law.
Treating the 2011 SPDI Rules as the current standard after 13 May 2027, when section 43A is removed.
Reading only the Act and missing the Rules, which carry the operating detail.

recall.q: When did the Act receive Presidential assent?
recall.a: 11 August 2023, as Act No. 22 of 2023.

recall.q: Which provisions took effect on 13 November 2025?
recall.a: The definitions, the Data Protection Board (sections 18 to 26) and the RTI amendment (section 44(3)).

recall.q: When does the Act reach processing outside India?
recall.a: When it is in connection with offering goods or services to Data Principals within India.

recall.q: What replaced the old regime on 13 May 2027?
recall.a: The DPDP Act and Rules, with section 44(2) removing section 43A of the IT Act.

sections.title: The key roles
sections.big_idea: The Principal owns the rights, the Fiduciary owns the duties, and the Processor works **under contract**, with accountability staying with you.
in_plain_words: A Data Principal is the person the data describes, and includes a parent or guardian for children and some persons with disabilities. The Data Fiduciary decides the purpose and means of processing. For most NGOs that is you. A Data Processor acts on your instruction and needs a contract with you.

Three other roles complete the picture. A Significant Data Fiduciary is notified by the government and carries extra duties. A Consent Manager is a registered platform for managing consent. The Data Protection Board enforces, and appeals go to the Appellate Tribunal. **Map these roles onto your own flagship programme.**

left.title: Data Fiduciary
items: Decides why and how data is used

key_terms.meaning: Person whose data it is; holds the rights.
Significant Data Fiduciary notified by the government.
Registered platform for giving and withdrawing consent.
A vendor's vendor, which must also be under contract.
The Appellate Tribunal for appeals from the Board.

worked_example.title: Map a nutrition NGO
worked_example.setup: A district nutrition NGO enrols a mother and her child, collects forms on a mobile survey app, and the app is hosted on a cloud service.
steps: The mother is a Data Principal.
Her child under 18 is also a Data Principal, represented by the mother or guardian.
The NGO decides what to collect and why, so it is the Data Fiduciary.
The survey app is a Data Processor and needs a contract. The cloud host behind it is a sub-processor in the chain.
The NGO's grievance officer is the contact point, and the Board is the regulator if a complaint escalates.
worked_example.answer: One NGO, one Fiduciary role, two processors in a chain, and a named grievance contact to close the first gap.

mistakes: Assuming that hiring a vendor moves your liability to the vendor.
Handling a vendor with no written contract, which the Act requires.
Forgetting that a child's rights are exercised by a parent or guardian.
Expecting to be notified as an SDF when the status is aimed at large, high-risk handlers.

recall.q: Who is the Data Fiduciary in most NGO work?
recall.a: The NGO itself, since it decides why and how data is processed.

recall.q: What three extra duties does an SDF carry?
recall.a: A Data Protection Officer based in India, an independent data auditor and periodic DPIAs.

recall.q: What does the Data Protection Board not do?
recall.a: It does not make rules. The Central Government makes the Rules.

recall.q: Under which section does an appeal lie to the Appellate Tribunal?
recall.a: Section 29.

sections.title: Consent & notice
sections.big_idea: Consent counts only if it follows a clear notice and is **free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous**.
in_plain_words: Consent is the main lawful basis, and it must meet a strict standard. Before or when you ask, give an itemised notice: what data, why, how to use rights, how to complain, in English or an Eighth Schedule language. A bad notice such as 'I agree to the terms' fails every test.

Consent can be withdrawn as easily as it was given, and withdrawal works forward only. For anyone under 18 you need verifiable parental consent, and tracking or targeted advertising directed at children is prohibited. Legitimate uses are narrow exceptions. **Separate essentials from optional uses** like photos so people can decline the optional parts.

diagram.note: silence, pre-ticked boxes and bundled consent do not count

key_terms.meaning: A plain statement of fields, purpose, rights and complaint route.
Consent of a parent or guardian, with reasonable steps to verify.
A defined case where processing needs no separate consent.
One tick covering unrelated uses; not valid.
Ending consent; forward-looking only.

worked_example.title: Fix a bad notice
worked_example.setup: A form says 'I agree to the terms and conditions.' Rewrite it using the deck's five notice items.
steps: What: name the fields, for example name, phone and household income.
Why: state the purpose, for example to check eligibility for the livelihoods grant.
Rights: say how to see, correct, erase or withdraw, and give a contact name.
Complaint: say how to complain to you and to the Board.
Language: provide it in the language the person reads, and unbundle photos and mailing lists into separate ticks.
worked_example.answer: A short notice naming fields, purpose, rights and contact in the local language, with optional uses on separate tick boxes.

mistakes: Using pre-ticked boxes or treating silence as agreement.
Bundling photos and case studies into the consent needed to receive the service.
Implying that refusing means losing the aid, which makes consent unfree.
Publishing a child's photo without verifiable parental consent for that specific use.

recall.q: What must an itemised notice tell the person?
recall.a: The data collected, the purpose, how to exercise rights, how to complain, in a language they understand.

recall.q: Does withdrawal make earlier processing unlawful?
recall.a: No. Withdrawal is forward-looking.

recall.q: How old must a person be to give their own consent under the Act?
recall.a: 18. Under that age a parent or guardian gives verifiable consent.

recall.q: Name two legitimate uses without separate consent.
recall.a: Any two of: voluntarily provided data, State benefits, legal obligations, medical emergencies, disasters, employment purposes.

sections.title: Rights & duties of the Data Principal
sections.big_idea: Four rights need a **workflow your team can run**: receive, verify, locate, act, record and reply.
in_plain_words: People can ask for a summary of their data and who it was shared with (Section 11), correction and erasure (Section 12), a grievance channel with a timely response (Section 13), and to nominate someone to act for them (Section 14). They also have duties under Section 15, such as not impersonating or filing false complaints.

Every right depends on knowing where the data sits. Verify identity before releasing or changing anything, log the date received and due, and acknowledge quickly. **Check the exact prescribed period** before you publish a firm commitment, since the Rules are phasing in.

key_terms.meaning: Section 11: a summary of data and who it was shared with.
Section 12: fix, complete or delete data.
Section 13: a channel and a timely response.
Section 14: someone to act on death or incapacity.
Individuals must act truthfully; penalty up to ₹10,000.

worked_example.title: Count the copies for an erasure
worked_example.setup: A woman asks to be removed from all records. The deck lists where her data sits.
steps: Excel file: 1 copy.
Mobile app: 1 copy, and the printed log book: 1 copy.
Two staff email inboxes: 2 copies, plus the submitted donor report: 1.
Excel, app and log book: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Inboxes and donor report: 2 + 1 = 3. Total places to check: 3 + 3 = 6.
Delete from active systems, instruct the processor, shred the log-book entry, and explain what the law requires you to keep.
worked_example.answer: Six places to deal with, and a written reply saying what was deleted and what must be retained.

mistakes: Releasing data before checking who is asking.
Having no data map, so a deletion request cannot be completed.
Erasing from the main database and forgetting backups, inboxes and paper files.
Ignoring a nomination because it is rare.

recall.q: Which section gives the right to access?
recall.a: Section 11.

recall.q: What should you do first when a rights request arrives?
recall.a: Verify the requester's identity.

recall.q: What penalty applies to a Data Principal who breaches their duties?
recall.a: Up to ₹10,000 under the Schedule.

recall.q: Why does the deck say a grievance process is your first line of defence?
recall.a: Individuals are generally expected to use it before going to the Board.

sections.title: Obligations of the Data Fiduciary
sections.big_idea: Collect less, **secure it, tell people and the Board of a breach within 72 hours**, and delete on time.
in_plain_words: The core duties are purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, reasonable security, breach notification, retention limits, and contracts with processors. Cutting fields and keeping data accurate cost nothing. Security is proportionate: individual accounts, encryption, backups, and locked cabinets are within reach of any NGO.

A breach triggers two notices, one to affected people without delay and a detailed report to the Board within 72 hours of becoming aware. SDFs add a DPO, an auditor and DPIAs. Cross-border transfer is allowed unless a country is restricted. **You can delegate processing but never accountability.**

diagram.caption: six duties that run through daily work

key_terms.meaning: Proportionate technical and organisational safeguards.
Unauthorised access, disclosure, loss or destruction.
Starts when you become aware of the breach.
Periodic Data Protection Impact Assessment for SDFs.
Stricter sector rules that still apply to some data.

worked_example.title: Run the breach clock
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a coordinator tells the director at 6 pm on a Monday that a laptop holding 6,000 records has been stolen.
steps: The clock starts at awareness, so 6 pm Monday is the start.
The Rules give 72 hours, and 72 ÷ 24 = 3 days.
The Board report is due by 6 pm on Thursday.
Affected people must be told without delay, and the plan should say who tells them.
worked_example.answer: Three days from awareness: a detailed report to the Board by Thursday 6 pm, with people notified sooner.

mistakes: Starting the 72-hour clock after the investigation ends. It starts at awareness.
Calling a breach only a hacking event. Loss, destruction and disclosure count too.
Using free survey tools with no contract with the vendor.
Collecting caste, religion or health fields out of habit.

recall.q: Who must be told of a personal data breach?
recall.a: The affected Data Principals and the Data Protection Board.

recall.q: How are cross-border transfers regulated?
recall.a: Allowed by default, except to countries or territories the government restricts.

recall.q: What should a processor contract cover?
recall.a: Purpose limits, security, confidentiality, breach notice to you, deletion on request and exit, and sub-processor controls.

recall.q: Which duty carries the highest penalty ceiling?
recall.a: Reasonable security safeguards, up to ₹250 crore.

sections.title: Enforcement & penalties
sections.big_idea: The Board enforces through complaints and inquiry, with **ceilings from ₹10,000 to ₹250 crore** and an appeal route.
in_plain_words: A complaint usually moves from your own grievance process to the Board, then inquiry, order and penalty, then appeal. The Board sets penalties within the Schedule, weighing nature, gravity and duration, the type of data, whether harm resulted, and what you did to mitigate. Most trouble stops at the grievance stage.

Voluntary undertakings under Section 32 offer an off-ramp, and appeals under Section 29 go to the Tribunal. The worked cases show an unencrypted laptop and children's photos used for sponsorship. **Concealment is itself penalised**, and cooperation counts in your favour.

key_terms.meaning: The maximum for a category; the Board sets the actual figure.
Section 32 promise to remedy a failure, binding once accepted.
Hears appeals from the Board under Section 29.
Steps you take to limit harm; the Board counts them.
Reusing data for a purpose the person was not told.

worked_example.title: Read the penalty schedule
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's maximum penalties to compare the failures in the two worked cases.
steps: The stolen unencrypted laptop is a security failure: ceiling ₹250 crore.
The sponsorship photo campaign is a children's data failure: ceiling ₹200 crore.
The gap between the two ceilings is 250 − 200 = 50 crore.
The security ceiling is five times the residual category: 250 ÷ 50 = 5.
These are ceilings. The Board weighs gravity, volume, harm and mitigation before setting an amount.
worked_example.answer: Security carries the highest ceiling at ₹250 crore, five times the ₹50 crore for other breaches.

mistakes: Hiding a breach, which is penalised up to ₹200 crore.
Reading the ₹250 crore figure as the fine for any slip.
Believing a Board order cannot be appealed.
Posting identifiable children's photos with school tags for fundraising.

recall.q: What is the maximum penalty for failing to notify a breach?
recall.a: Up to ₹200 crore.

recall.q: What triggers Board action in practice?
recall.a: Usually a complaint or a known breach. The Board does not run random audits.

recall.q: What does a voluntary undertaking do?
recall.a: It lets the Board accept a promise to remedy a failure instead of imposing a penalty, unless it is later breached.

recall.q: Who hears appeals from Board orders?
recall.a: The Appellate Tribunal, performed by TDSAT, with onward challenge to higher courts.

sections.title: What your NGO must do now
sections.big_idea: Seven steps in **90 days** build a strong baseline, starting with the data map.
in_plain_words: The steps are a data map, lawful consent forms and notices, a retention and deletion policy, a breach-response plan, fixed processor contracts, a named grievance officer, and staff training. The data map comes first because everything else builds on knowing what you hold and where.

The 90-day checklist groups them into see it, fix it and sustain it. Do the visible-risk items first: open links, unencrypted laptops and missing contracts. A small team can do this in a quarter. **Momentum beats perfection**, and the deck reminds you to take legal advice before any decision with real consequences.

children.label: Days 1 to 30: See it
items: Sweep for open links, weak locks

children.label: Days 31 to 60: Fix it
items: Put missing vendor contracts in place

key_terms.meaning: An inventory of what you hold, where, who sees it and how long.
A period and a deletion date for each data type.
A one-page plan: detect, contain, assess, notify, learn.
The named person handling complaints and rights requests.
A log of requests with dates and outcomes.

worked_example.title: Date the plan
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a two-person team starts the 90-day plan on day 1 and builds a data map for a beneficiary survey.
steps: Phase one ends at day 30, phase two at 30 + 30 = 60, and phase three at 60 + 30 = 90.
Data map row: type is beneficiary survey; fields are name, phone, household income.
Add purpose (eligibility check, consent), location (laptop, cloud app, paper), access (two named staff) and sharing (survey app vendor).
Add retention: keep through the programme and reporting, then delete everywhere, including backups.
worked_example.answer: A 90-day calendar and a first data-map row with seven columns completed.

mistakes: Starting with policies before building the data map.
Training only some staff. Field workers, data entry, finance, HR and volunteers all handle data.
Deleting from the main database but not from backups, inboxes and paper.
Leaving free tools with no contract in the processing chain.

recall.q: Why is the data map step one?
recall.a: You cannot protect, retain or erase data you cannot locate.

recall.q: What are the five steps of a breach-response plan?
recall.a: Detect and escalate, contain, assess, notify, learn.

recall.q: What should a good consent form do about optional uses?
recall.a: Unbundle them with their own tick boxes so people can decline without losing the service.

recall.q: What does the deck say culture adds to policies?
recall.a: Policies sit in a drawer, but culture travels to the field.

notes.3: Use the eight outcomes as a self-test at the end. Read the first one closely: the duties **apply on 13 May 2027**, so you are preparing for a date before any fine can arrive. Come back to this slide after Part 10 and tick off what you can now do.
notes.4: Seven reasons are listed. Choose the two your board will care about most and lead with those. For a donor-funded NGO that is usually the grant condition and the penalty. The slide's last line is the good news: **most of what the law asks costs little**.
notes.5: Check the right-hand column before you worry about skills. You need no lawyer, no software budget and no privacy training. The test on the slide is simple: if you write down a **name, phone number, photo, health status or bank detail**, the course is for you.
notes.6: Treat this table as a map of the ten parts. Parts 3 to 5 give you vocabulary, parts 6 to 8 give you the rules, part 9 shows what goes wrong and part 10 is the to-do list. If you are short of time, read part 10 and then follow its links backwards.
notes.7: Learn these six terms first, since every later slide uses them. The shortcut: the **Principal is the person, the Fiduciary is you, the Processor is your vendor**. Consent needs all four qualities on the slide, and the Board is the regulator that enforces.
notes.8: Memorise the three dates in this order: **13 November 2025** for the Board, **13 November 2026** for consent managers, and **13 May 2027** for the duties, rights and penalties. The seven principles at the bottom are the checklist behind every later slide.
notes.9: Answer truthfully in pencil, one statement at a time. Each 'no' is a gap this course closes. Three or more puts you where most Indian NGOs stand today. **Keep your score**, then take the same test after your 90-day plan to see what moved.
notes.10: Read the 'is not' column as a warning label. This course orients you; it does not replace legal advice. When a decision carries real risk to a person or a large penalty, **confirm the current text of the Act** and ask a qualified lawyer, as the golden rule says.
notes.11: Walk through your own organisation row by row. Mark which of these six sources you hold and write the most sensitive field in each. The last line sets the tone: the Act asks you to manage data **deliberately instead of by accident**.
notes.13: Study the scenario for its cause. A single sharing setting, 'anyone with the link', exposed bank numbers and transfer amounts. Convenience defaults cause most leaks and cost almost nothing to fix. **Check your own spreadsheets' sharing settings today.**
notes.14: Here the harm is physical. A survivor's address or her decision to seek help can bring renewed violence. Two controls from the slide apply immediately: store case files so only those who need them can open them, and **do not record details you do not strictly need**.
notes.15: The lesson is purpose limitation in a concrete form. Clients agreed to testing and support. They never agreed to appear in a donor report. Before you use any photo or log for **a purpose different from the original one**, get fresh, specific consent.
notes.16: Use the table to rank your own data by harm. The Act applies one standard to everything, but your ethics should not. The rule of thumb at the bottom is a good test: **the higher the harm, the stronger your reason to collect the field at all**.
notes.17: Read this as the ethical case behind the legal one. The power imbalance point matters most: people often cannot refuse data collection if aid depends on it, so **the duty of protection falls on you**. Sector standards already required this before the Act.
notes.18: Trust affects data quality as well as reputation. Where people fear misuse they give false ages, hide income and invent phone numbers, and your evidence rots. **Protecting data protects your findings.** Use this argument when someone calls privacy a compliance cost.
notes.19: Remember three points about Puttaswamy: nine judges, unanimous, and a **test of lawful, legitimate aim and proportionate**. That test reappears in the Act. For your NGO the practical meaning is that a beneficiary's data is part of their constitutional rights.
notes.20: Keep the sizes in proportion. The ₹250 crore and ₹200 crore figures are ceilings aimed at large handlers, and the Board weighs gravity before setting a figure. The 'no floor' tile is the one to remember: **no exemption for small or non-profit bodies**.
notes.21: Follow the logic of the six reasons. Voluntary codes left beneficiaries without remedy, digitisation raised the stakes and Puttaswamy made a statute expected. The takeaway sentence is the one to quote: **protecting data is now a duty you can be held to**.
notes.23: Apply the identifiability test to your own list. If a record can be linked to a living person, even through another dataset, it counts. Notice the 'still personal' column: **a beneficiary ID tied to a name list is personal data**, and so is a recognisable photo.
notes.24: The Act has no separate 'sensitive' category, so health data, caste and location data meet the same duties as a name. That is not permission to relax. The slide's practical advice is to **judge each field by the harm a leak would cause**. Children are the one group singled out.
notes.25: Processing covers every step from the moment a field worker types a name into a phone. The five-stage line collect, store, use, share, delete is **a memory aid for the next slide**. Notice that deleting is itself processing, so do it lawfully.
notes.26: Use the questions in the middle column as an audit. For each form or system, ask them at every stage. The design principle is the useful bit: **decide the deletion rule when you design the collection form**, before the data spreads across five systems.
notes.27: Learn the three states by example. 'HH-0421' with a lookup table is pseudonymised and still personal because it is reversible. Only true anonymisation leaves the law. For reports, **aggregate to groups large enough that nobody stands out**.
notes.28: Check what 'digital' covers. Paper that you later type into Excel is in scope, so almost all NGO data is. A handwritten book that is never digitised sits outside the Act but ethics still apply. **Do not rely on the paper loophole**, as the slide advises.
notes.29: Use this table when a European funder asks if you are 'GDPR-aligned'. Note the three main differences: no special category, a legitimate-use list in place of six bases, and a **child threshold of 18**. Meeting the DPDP gets you most of the way and leaves a few gaps.
notes.30: Learn the seven principles through the memory aid on the slide: collect what you need, for a reason you told them, keep it safe and accurate, delete when done, and **be able to show you did**. The last part, accountability, is what auditors and donors check first.
notes.31: Match each myth with its reality and note which is most common in your sector. The reassurance at the bottom is useful for small teams: the Act scales **how much you must do**, but never whether the core duties apply. A spreadsheet of personal data counts as a database.
notes.33: Read the history as a shortlist: 2011 SPDI Rules, 2017 Puttaswamy, 2018 Srikrishna Committee, 2019 Bill withdrawn in 2022, 2023 Act, 2025 Rules. The takeaway explains why the Act feels short: it is **principles-based, with detail in the Rules**.
notes.34: Treat this as a runway with three stages. The Board and definitions started on **13 November 2025**, consent managers follow on 13 November 2026, and the main duties, rights, exemptions and penalty powers arrive on 13 May 2027. The content of your duties is already fixed.
notes.35: Use the first four rows to decide whether you are covered, and the last two to see how it is enforced. The key phrase is 'decide how data is used', which includes trusts and societies. **Anonymised data and purely personal use fall outside.**
notes.36: If your beneficiaries live in India, assume the Act applies, whatever country holds your servers or head office. International NGOs serving India from abroad are drawn in. The outsourcing carve-out on the slide is narrow, so **do not expect it to fit domestic work**.
notes.37: Read the right-hand column before relying on any exemption. The research exemption is the one NGOs most hope for, and it is conditional: it fails if the data is used for decisions about a specific person. **When in doubt, treat the core duties as applying.**
notes.38: Bookmark the three commencement groups of Rules: Rules 1, 2 and 17 to 21 in force since 13 November 2025, Rule 4 from 13 November 2026, and the operational rules from 13 May 2027. The slide ends with advice worth following: **confirm the latest dates before acting**.
notes.39: Use the structure to find things in the Act. As an NGO you will spend most of your time in the Data Fiduciary obligations and the Data Principal rights, which are Parts 8 and 7 of this course. **The Schedule holds the penalty ceilings.**
notes.40: Treat the right-hand column as a task menu. Each row can be assigned to a person, given a date and ticked off. If you cannot name the owner of a row, **that principle is your first gap**. Compliance looks like this in daily practice.
notes.41: Read the three columns for the shift in tone: from sensitive-data-only rules to all personal data, from vague consent to withdrawable consent, from no regulator to a Board. The net-effect paragraph gives a date to remember: **section 44(2) removes section 43A on 13 May 2027**.
notes.43: Your beneficiaries, their families, donors, volunteers, applicants and staff are all Data Principals. Rights belong to them. The mindset shift on the slide is the one to hold onto: you are **the steward of the data and never its owner**.
notes.44: The test at the bottom decides your role: if you decide what is collected and what happens to it, you are the Fiduciary. Remember that **accountability cannot be outsourced**. Two organisations in a consortium can both be Fiduciaries.
notes.45: List every third party that touches your data, then check each for a written contract. The Act requires one, and you remain liable if the processor leaks. Include **sub-processors**, since the chain of contracts must run all the way down.
notes.46: Most NGOs will never be notified as an SDF, so treat this slide as awareness. The three extra duties are a Data Protection Officer in India, an independent auditor and periodic DPIAs. A **lighter version of each is good practice** for any size.
notes.47: A consent manager is a registered dashboard where a person manages all consents. Its obligations start on 13 November 2026, so the market is young. Your job for now: **keep consent records so you could honour a withdrawal that arrives through one**.
notes.48: Learn the Board by what triggers it: complaints, government references, court directions and breach reports. The grievance-first point is your practical protection. A working grievance process is **the way to stop a complaint reaching the Board at all**.
notes.49: Follow the chain on the slide: your grievance process, the Board, the Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT under Section 29), then the courts. Section 32 gives an off-ramp, the voluntary undertaking. The slide's point is that **prevention costs far less than any step in the chain**.
notes.50: Do the mapping exercise for your flagship programme. The slide shows a mother, her child, the NGO, the survey app and its cloud host, each with a role. If you cannot name your processor and its contract, **that is your first gap to close**.
notes.51: Use this table as a one-page cheat sheet. The column that matters most is 'Decides purpose?': only the Fiduciary and the SDF say yes. The one-line summary at the bottom is worth saying aloud: **Principal owns the rights, Fiduciary owns the duties**.
notes.53: Learn the five qualities as a checklist: free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous. The power-imbalance warning is the key point for aid work. Separate the essentials of the service from the optional extras, and **let people decline the extras without losing the service**.
notes.54: Use the five bullet points as the outline of your notice: what, why, how to use rights, how to complain, in a language they understand. Compare the bad and good examples at the bottom. **Name the fields**, since 'your details' is too vague.
notes.55: Make withdrawal as easy as giving consent, with a named person or number on the form. Remember it works forward only, so past processing stays lawful. When someone withdraws, **tell your processors to stop and delete**, and explain any consequence plainly.
notes.56: The age is 18. Use this to review any programme that touches children: education, nutrition, child protection, sponsorship. Photos count as personal data, so a published image needs **verifiable parental consent for that specific use**, plus no tracking and no targeting.
notes.57: Guardian consent applies only where a person with a disability has a lawful guardian. Many give their own consent. The most useful lines for practice are 'dignity first' and 'document the basis': **involve the person, and record who consented and on what authority**.
notes.58: Treat these six legitimate uses as narrow exceptions. They help in emergencies, legal duties and employment, but for ordinary programme data **consent is still your safest basis**. If you find yourself reaching for a legitimate use to skip consent, stop and ask why.
notes.59: Read the 'catch' column first. The research exemption is lost if the data is used to decide about individuals, such as who gets a benefit. Publicly available data excludes data that merely leaked. **If your data drives decisions about people, apply the full duties.**
notes.60: The four-step line shows what a person can do through a consent manager: sign up, grant, review, withdraw. You will probably not run one, but you should be ready to **honour consents and withdrawals that arrive through such a platform** once the market forms.
notes.61: Use this as a field-staff briefing. The six 'do' items form a script: explain the purpose in the local language, separate optional uses, record the answer. The honesty test at the bottom is a simple check: **read your notice aloud to the person**.
notes.63: Prepare for the access request by asking whether you could pull together everything you hold on one person within a week. Note that you must give identities of others you shared with. **Verify the requester first**, since releasing data to an impostor is itself a breach.
notes.64: The hard part of erasure is knowing where every copy is, which is why the data map comes first. Correction, completion and erasure should flow to processors and backups where feasible. **Write down what you changed and when** as proof you complied.
notes.65: Publish a named grievance contact and a log of complaints. The Fiduciary must respond within the period the Rules set. Remember the deck's own line: a responsive process is **your first line of defence** against a complaint reaching the Board.
notes.66: Nomination is rare, but a process that collapses when a nominee appears is a weakness. Verify the nominee's authority just as you would verify a requester. You need no elaborate system, only **awareness and a willingness to honour a valid nomination**.
notes.67: The five-step flow is the template to copy into your procedures: receive, verify, locate, act, record and reply. Each step relies on the data map. A rights workflow turns **a legal right into a service your team can deliver**.
notes.68: The Act also places duties on individuals, which matters when you help beneficiaries file requests. Encourage accurate claims. The penalty for breaching these duties goes up to ₹10,000, and the practical point is that **rights come with a duty of honesty**.
notes.69: Set an internal service standard now, such as acknowledging within days and resolving within weeks, and log the dates received and due. The slide's caution matters: **confirm the exact prescribed period before publishing a firm commitment**.
notes.70: Count the places this woman's data lives: Excel, an app, a printed log book, two inboxes and a donor report. The lesson is stark: **you cannot honour erasure if you do not know where the copies are**. Explain plainly what you must keep and why.
notes.71: Use the table as a quick reference and notice the section numbers: 11, 12, 13 and 14 for rights, 15 for duties. All of it applies from 13 May 2027. **Rights are paired with a duty of honesty**, and both are balanced by the Fiduciary's obligations in the next part.
notes.73: Interrogate every field on your form with one question: does the purpose fail without it? If not, cut it. Treat eligibility, photos, research and mailing lists as separate purposes with separate consents. **Data you never collected cannot leak.**
notes.74: Accuracy matters when data decides something about a person, such as a benefit. Read details back at collection and make correction easy. **Duplicates cause errors and make erasure hard**, so keep one record per person and update it instead of adding conflicting entries.
notes.75: Start with the cheap basics: individual accounts, passwords, encryption on laptops and phones, backups, locked cabinets. 'Reasonable' scales with your size and the sensitivity of your data. Security is **the most heavily penalised duty**, so do this first.
notes.76: The breach duty has two audiences: notify affected people without delay and report to the Board within 72 hours. The clock starts the moment you become aware and keeps running during your investigation. **A breach includes loss and destruction as well as hacking.**
notes.77: Decide a retention period for each data type when you design the form. Where audit or grant rules require records, keep the minimum for the required time, then delete. Think of old data as **a liability with no value**, and put a deletion schedule on the calendar.
notes.78: The three SDF extras are a DPO based in India, an independent auditor and periodic DPIAs. Most NGOs are unlikely to be notified. The practical suggestion is **a lighter version for everyone**: a named data lead, an annual self-review and a simple risk assessment.
notes.79: Transfers abroad are allowed unless the government restricts a destination. Using a foreign cloud service is a transfer, so ask your vendors where the data physically sits and record the answer. **Sending data abroad never moves your responsibility with it.**
notes.80: Use the list of contract terms as a checklist: purpose limits, security, confidentiality, breach notice to you, deletion on request, sub-processors. The common gap is free tools with no contract. You may **delegate processing, but never accountability**.
notes.81: Convert each row into a yes or no question and answer it at your next leadership meeting. The slide suggests a standing quarterly review. Rows you cannot answer with a confident yes are **your agenda items for the next quarter**.
notes.83: Know what the Board does and what it does not. It investigates, directs urgent measures, sets penalties within the Schedule and can accept undertakings. It does not write the rules. Its powers apply from **13 May 2027**, and proceedings are mostly online.
notes.84: Trace the five steps and notice where you can intervene. Most trouble stops at step one, your own grievance response. A prompt, fair reply **usually prevents escalation entirely**, which is cheaper than any inquiry, order or appeal.
notes.85: Read the penalty table as a ranking of seriousness: security at ₹250 crore, then breach notification and children's data at ₹200 crore, SDF duties at ₹150 crore and everything else at ₹50 crore. These are ceilings. **Security and honest breach reporting are the two duties to get right first.**
notes.86: Link each penalty to a behaviour you can recognise: an open link or unencrypted laptop is a security failure, silence after a breach is a notification failure, a child's photo without consent is a children's failure. The Board also weighs your **real efforts to mitigate**.
notes.87: The voluntary undertaking is an off-ramp: you promise to fix a problem and the Board may accept it in place of a contested penalty. Once accepted it is binding, and breaking it reopens the penalty. **Coming forward is rewarded over concealment.**
notes.88: The appeal route runs from the Board to the Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) and then to the higher courts. It shows that orders are reviewable. But the closing warning is the real point: **reaching an appeal means cost and reputational damage have already happened**.
notes.89: Work the stolen-laptop case as an exercise: the failure was an unencrypted device with 6,000 records, the clock started at awareness, and both people and the Board needed notice. **Two avoidable choices created the severity**, and both are fixed before a crisis.
notes.90: This case shows purpose creep: photos taken for records were used for fundraising. Naming a child and tagging the school also creates a child-protection risk. The fix is consent for each use, or better still **non-identifying images and no location tags**.
notes.91: Take each myth and say the fact aloud. The one with the highest stakes is concealment: hiding a breach is itself a penalised failure up to ₹200 crore. The balance paragraph is useful with boards: **enforcement is real but proportionate**.
notes.93: Build this map before anything else, because every later step relies on it. Seven columns are enough: type, fields, purpose, location, access, sharing, retention. Start with one spreadsheet filled by your team in a week. **You cannot protect what you cannot locate.**
notes.94: Draft one master consent and notice template and adapt it per programme. Include purpose, plain local language, unbundled optional uses, the rights, a grievance contact and a way to record consent. The quality test is to read it aloud: **if it embarrasses you, rewrite it**.
notes.95: Give every row of your data map a retention period tied to purpose and law. Then schedule deletion on a calendar and include backups, the survey app, inboxes and paper. The culture shift is the lesson: **old data is a liability with no asset value**.
notes.96: Write the one-page breach plan before you need it. The five steps are detect, contain, assess, notify and learn. Name the person who receives internal reports. A plan on paper is what makes **a 72-hour deadline realistic**.
notes.97: List your vendors from the data map, then check each for a written contract that covers purpose, security, breach notice, deletion and sub-processors. The quiet risk is free survey apps and personal cloud drives. **Bring each under contract or replace it.**
notes.98: Name one person and give them real authority to find data and instruct staff. Publish the contact on forms, the website and the notice board. In a small team this can be one senior person's defined duty: **what matters is that it is named, resourced and known**.
notes.99: Teach habits using your own scenarios: the open link, the stolen laptop, the sponsorship photo. Cover everyone who touches data and refresh annually. The slide asks you to reward early reporting of mistakes, since **mistakes caught early can still be contained**.
notes.100: Use the three phases as your calendar: see it in days 1 to 30, fix it in days 31 to 60, sustain it in days 61 to 90. Start with the visible risks, open links, unencrypted laptops and missing contracts, then build policies. **Momentum beats perfection.**
notes.101: Read the questions before your board does. The answers are short and consistent: yes, you are covered; no, you do not need expensive software; record consent; delete old data unless you have a basis to keep it. The final answer gives the key dates in one place.
notes.102: Use this second myths table as a quiz for your team. The common thread at the bottom is the rule to apply: most myths **shrink the law's reach in wishful ways**. When unsure, assume the duty applies and act on that assumption.
notes.103: Read the Act's definitions and the Schedule first, then the Rules for operational detail. Check the latest version for any change to the dates. The closing line is a boundary: rely on this course for orientation, and **take qualified legal advice before any decision with real legal consequences**.
notes.104: Pick the three takeaways you will repeat to your board: you are covered, start with a map, prepare now. The remaining lines compress the course into habits. **Behind every record is a person who can be harmed by a leak**, and that is the reason to act.
